articles.title: Nick Reiner won't face death penalty in Rob, Michele Reiner murder case
articles.summary: Nick Reiner returns to court Tuesday as proceedings continue in the case involving the alleged killings of his parents, Rob and Michele Reiner.
articles.body: All eyes will be on Nick Reiner on Tuesday when he returns to court for the latest proceedings in his criminal case. Reiner is accused of killing his parents, Rob and Michele Reiner. Los Angeles County District Attorney Nathan J. Hochman announced Tuesday that his office will not pursue the death penalty against Reiner during a press conference ahead of his court hearing. "In deciding whether or not the DA's office was going to seek the death penalty, we have gone through a rigorous review where we look at the aggravating factors, as well as the mitigating factors – where we have spoken to the victims' family, we have spoken to prosecutors, law enforcement, and I've worked with the most senior people in the district attorney's office," Hochman told reporters Tuesday. "After a careful and thorough review of all these factors, the District Attorney's office will not be seeking the death penalty in this case. That means that the maximum sentence that Mr. Reiner will be looking at is life without the possibility of parole." NICK REINER INDICTED IN MURDERS OF PARENTS ROB, MICHELE REINER AT BRENTWOOD HOME Reiner was charged with two counts of murder and included special circumstance allegations of multiple murders and lying in wait after a grand jury indictment. Prosecutors also alleged he used a knife. "This was a profound betrayal by someone who was loved and trusted by the very people he is accused of killing," Los Angeles County District Attorney Hochman said at the time. During Tuesday's press conference, Hochman revealed Nick's siblings have petitioned for the grand jury transcripts to be sealed. "…they have expressed a strong desire for these transcripts to remain sealed," he told reporters. "And they basically have said that the disclosure to the public and the media of the details and evidence of the killing of their parents will cause them additional trauma and harm, and they have respectfully asked for the court to keep the transcript sealed." articles.body: British actor Johnny Flynn, 43, has opened up about his childhood and the bullying he experienced while studying at Winchester’s Pilgrims’ School. Flynn attended the boarding school from the age of seven after securing a choral scholarship.Recalling the experience in a new interview with Radio Times, the actor said it had a lasting impact on him. “It was quite traumatic for me,” he said. “I think they should all be burnt to the ground, I don’t think private schools should exist.”Flynn also revealed that being separated from his family at such a young age affected him psychologically. He developed “little nervous tics” and said it took him years to fully understand the mental toll the experience had taken on him.Johnny Flynn says therapy helped him understand ‘boarding school syndrome’Flynn said therapy eventually helped him make sense of the pain associated with his childhood. Describing the therapy as “brilliant”, he recalled reaching a point where he realised there was something deeper behind his experiences.“I suddenly thought, ‘God, there’s something quite painful about this.’ I learnt there was something called boarding school syndrome. And I’m good, I’m OK now,” Flynn said.Johnny Flynn to play Lucius Malfoy in HBO’s Harry Potter seriesFlynn will next be seen as Lucius Malfoy, the father of Harry Potter’s nemesis Draco Malfoy, in HBO’s highly anticipated television adaptation of the Harry Potter books. The character was previously played by Jason Isaacs in the film franchise.He is among several prominent British actors joining the new series. articles.title: Ed Sheeran Insists Dropping Macklemore Was Not His Decision: ‘I Am Not Complicit’
articles.summary: “There is a reason I do not use my professional platform for politics," the Loop Tour singer says, while condemning pain caused by "both sides" of Israel and...
articles.body:
Ed Sheeran shared his side of the story on Tuesday, a day after Macklemore was dropped from the Loop Tour for sharing his pro-Palestine stance onstage.

"Macklemore coming off tour was the promoter's decision. It was not mine. Macklemore's contract for the tour was with the promoter, not me," Sheeran explained. "I would never let down the fans who had made plans, nor would I abandon the touring crew and the other support acts and musicians who rely on me for work and to make a living."

The "Shape of You" singer's statement appears to corroborate both Macklemore and Robert Kraft's version of events after the rapper blamed the billionaire for his removal due to his "Free Palestine" messaging.

"I am appalled by the conflict between Israel and Palestine. The suffering and pain caused on both sides is a human tragedy," Sheeran began his Instagram message. "There are too many wars across the world causing immeasurable pain, none of which should be tolerated."

"After Macklemore's performances at my New Jersey shows, venues on my upcoming tour dates communicated that they would pull the shows if he was still supporting. I was informed that this stance was based on how Macklemore conveyed part of his message during his performance, rather than on everything that was said," he added. "I spoke with the venues at length all week to try and build a bridge. One of those people was Robert Kraft. I was also involved in direct talks with promoters along with activists on both side to try and find a mutual resolution for all, but the venue's and promoter's decision was final."

"Based on Macklemore's recent actions, material shared from the stage during Ed Sheeran's shows in New Jersey, and a broader history of antisemitic rhetoric and imagery that we believe has been deeply offensive and hurtful to the Jewish community, we determined that his participation in the Sept. 25 and 26 concerts at Gillette Stadium would cross that line," the New England Patriots owner shared in a Monday statement.

Macklemore was originally scheduled to open for eight more shows on Sheeran's tour, kicking back up Friday in Philadelphia. These updates come a week after the Israeli American Council condemned his pro-Palestine messaging , issuing a petition for his removal from the tour.

"I am not complicit. I have my personal views on this devastating conflict. Just because I choose not to speak publicly, it doesn't mean that I don't have them, and it doesn't mean I don't care. Nor does it mean I don't support causes in my own, personal way," Sheeran further insisted on Tuesday. "There is a reason I do not use my professional platform for politics — My audience includes young people, often children, of all backgrounds. Those who come to my shows do not expect a political forum. I respect Macklemore's strength of purpose to stand up and shout for what he believes. However, there is room for multiple approaches to same end: peace."

For his part, Macklemore made sure to point out that "Antisemitism is real" in his initial statement, while also noting that "more than 20,000 children have been killed in Gaza alone."

"Ed was in a f–ked up position. He knew it. His typical apolitical stance was being challenged in a way it never had been before," he wrote on Monday. "But he couldn't get past his public-facing 'I don't take sides.'"

"I didn't need 10 shows from Ed. I needed two. Two chances to stand in front of 90,000 people and say the words that somehow became too dangerous to say. Free Palestine," Macklemore concluded. "If those words cost me the stage, while turning the conversation back to Palestine, then it was the most successful tour I've been on."

articles.title: Vintage Violence is an absurdist crime thriller for phone addicts
articles.summary: The 2026 edition of the Toronto International Film Festival, or TIFF, included movies like Vintage Violence, Ken Russell’s The Devils in 4K, and Gentle Monster.
articles.body: There are a lot of movies that have tried to seamlessly integrate modern tech — text messages, livestreams, etc. — into their storytelling. Some of the most novel attempts have been in the genre space, like the Twitch-style horror flick Deadstream. But the most chaotic to date might just be Vintage Violence, an absurd crime thriller with lots of blood, jokes, and screentime. I was able to catch Vintage Violence, the latest from director Eugene Kotlyarenko, on my fifth day at the Toronto International Film Festival. Kotlyarenko has previously explored our hyper-connected culture in 2020’s Spree, a movie in which Stranger Things’ Joe Keery plays a rideshare driver who starts murdering passengers while livestreaming the crimes. But Vintage Violence takes things a step further by trying to replicate what it’s like to constantly be on your phone as the movie plays out. It’s a lot to take in, but I really enjoyed it. Unfortunately there isn’t a trailer yet to give you a better sense of how things work onscreen, but I’ll make sure to share it when they do release one. Vintage Violence was one of three films I took in on day 5 of TIFF 2026; the others were a 4K restoration of a cult classic and a devastating drama that’s on its way to Netflix. Here are my thoughts on all three. [Image: Vintage Violence No theatrical date yet From the premise alone you can tell this movie is ridiculous. Carter (Cole Sprouse), a disgraced MrBeast-style influencer, finds a cache of vintage Levi’s while livestreaming, and one of his fans, Izumi (Kiko Mizuhara), suggests he comes to Tokyo to sell the denim for some big cash. When he gets there, just about everyone is running some kind of scam — pretty quickly the yakuza get involved, including an enforcer with a prosthetic middle finger — and things play out like a toned-down, but still brutal and bloody, Takashi Miike film. But what really elevates Vintage Violence is the way it constantly displays what characters are doing on their phones right alongside the main film. That means everything from sending text messages to livestreaming to listening to whale sounds to relax. It can get chaotic and a challenge to follow — at one point I was trying to read the chat on a Kick stream while an action scene played out beside it — but that’s also kind of the point. [Media: Ken Russell’s The Devils In theaters on October 16th The Devils is one of those cult classics I’ve always meant to watch but never got around to. But this new 4K theatrical rerelease was the perfect excuse. First released in 1971, The Devils is a surreal and disturbing account of a witch trial in a small, independent town in 17th-century France. Run by an impossibly handsome priest (Oliver Reed) who openly defies a powerful cardinal, the town soon descends into pure hysteria following reports of demonic possession, which the church seizes on in order to oust the priest. This version is not only a remaster but also a director’s cut — it’s rated NC-17 — and while I can’t speak to what’s new since I hadn’t seen it before, I will say the film rarely shows its age, with enthralling and disturbing sequences merged with a poignant story about the dangers of mixing politics and religion. And in 4K the stark architecture and uncomfortable violence really pop on the big screen. [Media: Gentle Monster In theaters on October 30th; streaming on Netflix on November 18th Marie Kreutzer’s latest feature is a difficult watch. It follows a young family that is torn apart when the police arrive at their country home one day to seize the father’s digital devices as part of a CSAM investigation. The story is primarily centered on the mother, Lucy (Léa Seydoux), a pianist who struggles with accepting a truth that threatens to upend her entire world. Gentle Monster does a remarkable job of slowly taking you through Lucy’s complicated, messy, and constantly changing understanding of the situation, but what really makes it work is Seydoux’s raw and unnerving performance, which oscillates between wishing the problem would go away to doing anything she can to protect her son. It’s a great film, but one that’s certain to leave you unsettled.
